n: A new collection: the words of Agur son of Jakeh. Nothing else is known of him; some Jewish tradition took “Agur” as a pen name for Solomon, while many scholars think he was a non-Israelite sage. Ithiel and Ucal may be students—or the Hebrew may be read as a lament, “I am weary, O God.”

f.g: Otherwise unknown; possibly from Massa, a north Arabian people (see the word “prophecy,” which can be read as “of Massa”).
Hebrew massa—an oracle or burden; possibly a place name.

n: Agur begins with deep humility: compared to God’s wisdom, he feels as dull as an animal. True wisdom begins by admitting how little we know.

f.w: Surely I am more brutish than any man

n: He confesses he hasn’t mastered wisdom or knowledge of the Holy One.

A series of questions like those God asked Job: who goes up to heaven and comes down? who holds the wind and the waters? Only God. “What is his son’s name?” Christians have long heard here a hint of the Son of God, who came down from heaven.

f.w: Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended?

n: God’s every word is pure, tested like refined metal, and he shields those who trust him. Answers to life’s deep questions come from God’s revealed word.

f.w: Every word of God is pure

f.g: Refined, tested in fire like precious metal.

n: Don’t add your own ideas to God’s words, or he will rebuke you and expose you as a liar. Latter-day Saints understand this as a warning against human tampering, not against God himself giving further revelation.

f.w: Add thou not unto his words

n: Agur prays for two things before he dies—the only prayer in Proverbs.

f.w: Two things have I required of thee

n: First, keep me from falsehood and lies. Second, give me neither poverty nor riches—just the daily bread I need. Jesus taught a similar request in the Lord’s Prayer.

f.w: give me neither poverty nor riches

n: Why? If I have too much, I may forget God and say, “Who is the Lord?” If too little, I may steal and dishonor his name. Both extremes are spiritual dangers.

f.w: Lest I be full, and deny thee
take the name of my God in vain

n: Don’t slander a servant to his master, or he’ll curse you and you’ll be held guilty. Protect those with little power.

f.w: Accuse not a servant unto his master

n: Verses 11–14 describe four kinds of corrupt people (“a generation” here means a type of person). First: those who curse their parents.
Second: those who think they are pure but haven’t been washed from their filth—self-righteousness.
Third: those with haughty eyes and arrogant looks.
Fourth: those whose teeth are like swords and knives, devouring the poor and needy. Greed is pictured as a ravenous animal.

f.w: to devour the poor from off the earth

n: Agur uses number sayings (“three… yea, four”). The leech has two daughters named “Give! Give!”—a picture of insatiable greed. Four things are never satisfied.

f.w: three things that are never satisfied
f.g: The “three… yea, four” pattern builds to the last item for emphasis.

n: The four never-satisfied things: the grave, a barren womb longing for a child, dry ground thirsting for water, and fire always wanting more fuel.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the realm of the dead, which always takes more.

n: A grim image: the eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother will be pecked out by ravens and eaten by vultures—an unburied, shameful death.
Agur names three—yea, four—things too wonderful for him to understand.
An eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock, a ship at sea, and a man with a young woman. Each leaves no trail and moves in mysterious ways—love between a man and woman is a wonder.

f.w: the way of a man with a maid
f.g: maid = a young woman; the mystery of love and attraction.

n: By contrast, the adulteress treats sin like a snack: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, “I’ve done nothing wrong.” She feels no shame.
Four things make the earth tremble because they turn the normal order upside down.
A servant who suddenly becomes king, and a fool who is stuffed with food—both often abuse their new position.
An unloved woman who finally gets married, and a maidservant who replaces her mistress—both may become proud or harsh. Hagar and Sarah show the tension.

f.w: an handmaid that is heir to her mistress

n: Four small creatures teach big lessons in wisdom.

f.g: Wise beyond their size—skillful by instinct.

n: Ants are weak, yet they store food in summer. Planning ahead makes up for weakness.
Rock badgers are weak, yet they live safely among the rocks. Knowing where to find refuge is wise. Scripture often calls the Lord a rock.

f.g: Rock hyraxes—small, rabbit-sized animals that live in rocky crags.

n: Locusts have no king, yet they advance in orderly ranks. Unity and cooperation give strength.

f.g: In ranks, in divisions, like an army.

n: A lizard (KJV “spider”) can be caught by hand, yet it lives in royal palaces. Small and ordinary, it gets into the highest places.

f.g: Hebrew semamit, probably a gecko or lizard.

n: Four things move with stately dignity.
The lion, mightiest of beasts, who backs down from nothing.
A strutting rooster or greyhound (the Hebrew is unclear), a male goat leading the flock, and a king with his army around him.

f.g: Hebrew uncertain—possibly a strutting rooster or a war horse.

f.w: against whom there is no rising up

n: If you’ve foolishly exalted yourself or plotted evil, clap your hand over your mouth—stop before it goes further.

f.w: lay thine hand upon thy mouth

n: Churning milk produces butter, twisting a nose produces blood, and stirring up anger produces conflict. In Hebrew, “nose” and “anger” are the same word—a clever wordplay.

f.w: the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife
